Patient Vignette: David

David is a 37-year-old database administrator, a man whose life once revolved around the quiet, predictable order of server logs and query results. He presents as lean and watchful, with a habit of scanning the room before he sits down. He speaks in measured, precise sentences, as if he is still trying to structure the chaos of the last two years into something he can manage.

The traumatic event began eighteen months ago, on a Tuesday. David had been feeling tired for weeks, dismissing it as the result of late nights migrating a client's data system. Then came the chest pain during a morning run. He assumed it was heartburn. It was not. In the emergency room, a physician told him he had a pulmonary embolism-a massive clot in his left lung. The words "life-threatening" were used. David remembers the sensation of the oxygen mask against his face, the beeping of the monitors, the way the ceiling tiles looked like a grid of white squares he could count. He remembers thinking, This is a system failure. I am a system failure.

He was hospitalized for six days. The physical recovery was slow, but the real change happened inside. In the weeks after his discharge, David found himself unable to sleep without the lights on. He began checking his own pulse multiple times an hour, pressing two fingers to his wrist while standing in the server room at work. The first time he felt a skipped heartbeat, he left the office without telling anyone and drove to the emergency room. The doctor told him it was a benign palpitation. David did not believe him.

At work, his performance has deteriorated. He is a database administrator for a mid-sized logistics company, a job that once felt like a refuge of logic. Now, when he stares at a screen of SQL code, his mind drifts. He will catch himself thinking about the sensation of the IV line in his arm, the way the anticoagulant dripped cold into his vein. He has started to avoid the break room because the coffee machine makes a hissing sound that reminds him of the oxygen tank. He tells his colleagues he is fine, but he has taken more sick days in the past six months than in the previous five years combined.

His marriage did not survive. His ex-wife, a nurse, tried to be patient. She would find him standing in the bathroom at 3 AM, staring at his own reflection, pressing his hand to his chest. She would say, "You're fine, David. The scans were clear." He would hear the words, but they felt like static. The last fight was about a vacation. She wanted to go to the mountains. He could not bring himself to fly. He could not bring himself to be that far from a hospital. The divorce was finalized four months ago.

David now lives alone in a one-bedroom apartment with a fire escape he has memorized the route to. He keeps a first aid kit in his car, his desk drawer, and his nightstand. He has not exercised since the embolism, because every time his heart rate rises, he feels the ghost of the clot. He has stopped going to his follow-up appointments because the waiting room reminds him of the hospital hallway where a resident told him, "You're lucky to be alive." He does not feel lucky. He feels like he is still waiting for the other shoe to drop.

In session, David sits forward, hands clasped. He describes a recurring thought: My body is a ticking bomb. He does not say this dramatically. He says it like a fact, like a line of code he has written and cannot delete. He has stopped dating. He has stopped planning for retirement. He has stopped believing in the future, not because he is depressed, but because he is convinced the future will arrive with another ambulance.

He is here because his boss mandated a wellness check after a colleague found him hyperventilating in the server closet. David agreed to come, but he does not know if talking will help. He says, "I know the clot is gone. I know I'm fine. But I don't feel fine. I feel like I'm still in that bed." He looks at the clock on the wall, then back at the door. He is already calculating the fastest exit.
